segments.voice: Yesterday's line: honor the old. Confucius waited for the staffs; the Torah says rise. This week's lines come back in the games: the student, the householder, every day a practice, midway, stepping back, honor the old. Today, the last season.

segments.voice: A folder labeled 'if something happens': the passwords, the will, a note. Jacob's last days hold a blessing, not a folder. He's old and sick, his eyes dim with age, and his son Joseph brings in his two boys, Manasseh and Ephraim. Joseph sets the older one by Jacob's right hand, the hand meant for the firstborn. And Jacob crosses his arms, on purpose, and lays his right hand on the younger.
screen: `A FOLDER: IF SOMETHING HAPPENS.` → `JACOB, OLD AND NEARLY BLIND.` → `TWO GRANDSONS.` → `HE CROSSES HIS HANDS.`

segments.voice: Joseph tries to move his father's hand. Jacob refuses: "I know it, my son, I know it." The younger, he says, will be greater. And he blesses them with words that outlived him: "In thee shall Israel bless, saying, God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." That line is why, in Jewish homes on Friday night, parents can lay their hands on their sons' heads and say: may God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh. Daughters can be blessed with the names of Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah. A deathbed became a weekly practice. Then Jacob gathers all his sons and gives each a word, and the text says "he gathered up his feet into the bed, and yielded up the ghost." Here's the teaching, and today's word, the dying stage. In Jewish tradition the end of life is a time to bless, and to hand on what matters. Some Jews write an ethical will, a letter of values rather than property, and some readers hear Jacob's blessings as one. So the week's seasons close here. The student who serves. The householder who holds everyone up. The parent's daily mirror. The dark wood, midway. The house, handed on. The old, honored. And last, the blessing.

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write one line about how you'd want the end to be: who's near, and what you'd want to say to them. If thoughts of dying feel heavy or close today, skip this one and reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number. Then rest your hand on the page for the rest of the time.
The dying stage: the last season of life, kept as a practice, not only endured. Jacob spent it blessing the ones he loved, one by one, by name.
One more line for the week: the last practice, a blessing handed on by name. Day 1687, and that's the week.

howItsDone: In some Jewish homes on Friday night, parents bless their children, sons with Jacob's words from Genesis 48:20 (may God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh) and daughters with the names of the matriarchs. Some Jews also write an ethical will, a letter of values for those who come after.
